label: PYQ-style
stem: Give reasons: (i) zinc is not regarded as a transition element; (ii) $\ce{Cr^2+}$ is a strong reducing agent.
model_answer:
(i) Zn is [Ar]$3d^{10}4s^2$; its d subshell is completely filled in the atom and in $\ce{Zn^2+}$ ($3d^{10}$), so it has no partly filled d orbitals in any common oxidation state. [1]
(ii) $\ce{Cr^2+}$ ($3d^4$) changes to $\ce{Cr^3+}$ ($3d^3$), which has the stable half-filled $t_{2g}^3$ configuration; hence $E^\circ_{\ce{Cr^3+/Cr^2+}}$ is negative ($-0.41$ V) and $\ce{Cr^2+}$ readily loses an electron. [1]

scheme.step: (i) Zn is [Ar]$3d^{10}4s^2$; its d subshell is completely filled in the atom and in $\ce{Zn^2+}$ ($3d^{10}$), so it has no partly filled d orbitals in any common oxidation state.

(ii) $\ce{Cr^2+}$ ($3d^4$) changes to $\ce{Cr^3+}$ ($3d^3$), which has the stable half-filled $t_{2g}^3$ configuration; hence $E^\circ_{\ce{Cr^3+/Cr^2+}}$ is negative ($-0.41$ V) and $\ce{Cr^2+}$ readily loses an electron.

hint: (i) Look at the d configuration of Zn and Zn²⁺. (ii) Which stable configuration does Cr³⁺ have?

label: PYQ-style
stem: What is lanthanoid contraction? State its cause and two consequences.
model_answer:
**Lanthanoid contraction** is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of the lanthanoids from La to Lu. [1]
**Cause:** the 4f electrons shield one another from the nucleus very poorly, so the effective nuclear charge rises with atomic number. [1]
**Consequences:** (i) 4d and 5d elements of a group have almost the same radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm), so they occur together and are hard to separate; (ii) basic strength of the hydroxides decreases from $\ce{La(OH)3}$ to $\ce{Lu(OH)3}$. [½ + ½]

scheme.step: **Lanthanoid contraction** is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of the lanthanoids from La to Lu.
**Cause:** the 4f electrons shield one another from the nucleus very poorly, so the effective nuclear charge rises with atomic number.

**Consequences:** (i) 4d and 5d elements of a group have almost the same radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm), so they occur together and are hard to separate; (ii) basic strength of the hydroxides decreases from $\ce{La(OH)3}$ to $\ce{Lu(OH)3}$.

hint: Think about how well 4f electrons shield one another from the nucleus.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
Give reasons:
(i) Transition metals form coloured compounds.
(ii) $E^\circ$ for $\ce{Mn^3+/Mn^2+}$ (+1.57 V) is much more positive than for $\ce{Fe^3+/Fe^2+}$ (+0.77 V).
(iii) Actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids.
model_answer:
(i) Their ions have partly filled d orbitals; visible light is absorbed for d–d transitions and the complementary colour is seen. [1]
(ii) $\ce{Mn^2+}$ is $3d^5$ (half-filled, extra stable), so $\ce{Mn^3+}$ ($3d^4$) is easily reduced to it. $\ce{Fe^3+}$ is itself $3d^5$, so it is much less ready to be reduced to $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($3d^6$). [1]
(iii) In actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s levels have comparable energies, so more electrons can take part in bonding. [1]

scheme.step: (i) Their ions have partly filled d orbitals; visible light is absorbed for d–d transitions and the complementary colour is seen.

(ii) $\ce{Mn^2+}$ is $3d^5$ (half-filled, extra stable), so $\ce{Mn^3+}$ ($3d^4$) is easily reduced to it. $\ce{Fe^3+}$ is itself $3d^5$, so it is much less ready to be reduced to $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($3d^6$).
(iii) In actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s levels have comparable energies, so more electrons can take part in bonding.

hint: (i) d–d transitions. (ii) Compare the stability of d⁵ in Mn²⁺ and Fe³⁺. (iii) Compare 5f, 6d and 7s energies.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Describe, with equations, the preparation of $\ce{KMnO4}$ from pyrolusite ore ($\ce{MnO2}$). [2]
(b) Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of $\ce{Cr^3+}$ (Z = 24). [1]
(c) Give reasons: (i) $\ce{Cu+}$ is unstable in aqueous solution; (ii) the highest oxidation state of a transition metal is shown in its oxides and oxoanions. [2]
model_answer:
(a) $\ce{MnO2}$ is fused with KOH in the presence of air (or an oxidising agent such as $\ce{KNO3}$) to give green potassium manganate:
$\ce{2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2}$ $\ce{-> 2K2MnO4 + 2H2O}$ [1]
Manganate disproportionates in neutral or acidic solution to give purple permanganate:
$\ce{3MnO4^2- + 4H+}$ $\ce{-> 2MnO4- + MnO2}$ $\ce{+ 2H2O}$ [1]
(b) $\ce{Cr^3+}$: [Ar]$3d^3$, $n=3$; $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}=\sqrt{15}=\boxed{3.87\text{ BM}}$ [1]
(c)(i) $\ce{Cu+}$ disproportionates: $\ce{2Cu+(aq)}$ $\ce{-> Cu^2+(aq) + Cu(s)}$. The much more negative hydration enthalpy of $\ce{Cu^2+}$ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy of Cu. [1]
(ii) Oxygen is small and highly electronegative and can form multiple bonds with the metal, which stabilises high oxidation states (e.g. Mn(VII) in $\ce{MnO4-}$). [1]

scheme.step: (a) $\ce{MnO2}$ is fused with KOH in the presence of air (or an oxidising agent such as $\ce{KNO3}$) to give green potassium manganate: $\ce{2MnO2 + 4KOH + O2}$ $\ce{-> 2K2MnO4 + 2H2O}$
Manganate disproportionates in neutral or acidic solution to give purple permanganate: $\ce{3MnO4^2- + 4H+}$ $\ce{-> 2MnO4- + MnO2}$ $\ce{+ 2H2O}$

(c)(i) $\ce{Cu+}$ disproportionates: $\ce{2Cu+(aq)}$ $\ce{-> Cu^2+(aq) + Cu(s)}$. The much more negative hydration enthalpy of $\ce{Cu^2+}$ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy of Cu.
(ii) Oxygen is small and highly electronegative and can form multiple bonds with the metal, which stabilises high oxidation states (e.g. Mn(VII) in $\ce{MnO4-}$).

hint: Two stages: fuse to green manganate, then convert manganate to permanganate.

label: PYQ-style
stem: *In the laboratory the strength of an oxalic acid solution is found by titrating it against potassium permanganate. The oxalic acid is taken in the conical flask with dilute sulphuric acid and warmed to about 60 °C. Permanganate solution is run in from the burette. Each drop loses its colour until the end point, when one extra drop leaves a permanent pale pink.*

parts.stem: Why is no indicator added in this titration?
parts.model_answer: $\ce{KMnO4}$ is its own indicator: the purple $\ce{MnO4-}$ is reduced to almost colourless $\ce{Mn^2+}$, so the first excess drop gives a pink colour. [1]

scheme.step: $\ce{KMnO4}$ is its own indicator: the purple $\ce{MnO4-}$ is reduced to almost colourless $\ce{Mn^2+}$, so the first excess drop gives a pink colour.

parts.stem: Why is dilute sulphuric acid used, and not hydrochloric acid?
parts.model_answer: Permanganate oxidises HCl to chlorine, so some $\ce{KMnO4}$ would be used up by the acid and the result would be too high. [1]

scheme.step: Permanganate oxidises HCl to chlorine, so some $\ce{KMnO4}$ would be used up by the acid and the result would be too high.

parts.stem: Write the balanced ionic equation for the reaction. How many moles of oxalate ion are oxidised by one mole of $\ce{MnO4-}$?
parts.model_answer: $\ce{2MnO4- + 5C2O4^2-}$ $\ce{+ 16H+}$ $\ce{-> 2Mn^2+ + 10CO2}$ $\ce{+ 8H2O}$ [1] 5 mol of oxalate for 2 mol of permanganate, so **2.5 mol** per mole of $\ce{MnO4-}$. [1]

scheme.step: 5 mol of oxalate for 2 mol of permanganate, so **2.5 mol** per mole of $\ce{MnO4-}$.

hint: Count electrons: each $\ce{MnO4-}$ takes 5 in acid and each oxalate ion gives 2.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Define lanthanoid contraction and give its cause. [2]
(b) Zr (4d) and Hf (5d) have almost the same atomic radius and similar chemistry. Explain. [2]
(c) Give the ground-state configuration of Eu and explain why Eu$^{2+}$ is stable. [1]
model_answer:
*How much to write: about 14 lines · 10 minutes* **(a)** Lanthanoid contraction: the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii from La to Lu.
Cause: the 4f electrons shield poorly, so the effective nuclear charge rises across the series and pulls the outer shells in. **(b)** The contraction of the lanthanoids cancels the expected increase in size on going from the 4d to the 5d series, so Hf is about as small as Zr.
Hence Zr and Hf have very similar chemical properties and occur together in nature. **(c)** Eu: $\ce{[Xe]4f^7 6s^2}$. $\ce{Eu^2+}$ has a half-filled 4f⁷ shell, which is stable, so Eu shows the +2 state. :::tip Your answer must contain - effective nuclear charge and the reason 4f electrons shield poorly - the 4d–5d comparison with the reason for it - the half-filled 4f⁷ shell in (c) ::: **Marks are lost for:** saying radii increase across the series; no reason for shielding; no mention of 4d and 5d in (b).

scheme.step: (a) Definition: decrease in atomic and ionic radii across La to Lu
(a) Cause: poor shielding by 4f electrons, rising effective nuclear charge
(b) Contraction cancels the size increase; Zr and Hf have similar radii and chemistry
(c) Eu [Xe]4f7 6s2; Eu2+ has a stable half-filled 4f7 shell

hint: Two parts of (a): what happens to the size, and what causes it. For (b), compare what you expect when you go down a group with what happens in the lanthanoids.
